Disease Entity Meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD) is recognized by the following codes as per the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) nomenclature: * ICD-10:H02.89 * Short Description: Other specified disorders of eyelid Disease Meibomian glands or glandulae tarsales are large sebaceous glands in the eyelids that secrete lipids that form the superficial layer of tear film to protect against evaporation of the aqueous phase. These glands were first described in detail by German physician Heinrich Meibom (1638–1700) and were named after him (Fig 1).[1] Figure 1. Dr. Heinrich Meibom. Reprinted with permission of the Herzog August Bibliothek, Wolfenbüttel, Germany, Signatur B 100 There are about 25–40 meibomian glands in the human upper eyelid and about 20–30 in the lower eyelid, with respective lengths of about 5.5 mm and 2 mm in Caucasian eyes.[2] [3]Each gland in the upper eyelid consists of clusters of about 10–15 secretory acini. These secrete lipid material through small ductules via a central duct at the lid margin, contributing to the outermost layer of the tear film.[4] The contraction of the orbicularis muscle during blinking and the contraction of Riolan muscle at the terminal part of the ductal system generates mechanical force that facilitates the secretion of meibum.[5] Meibum contains over 100 major individual complex lipids, over 90 proteins, and electrolytes.[6] [7] Aging, diet, sex hormones, systemic and ocular surface inflammatory disorders, usage of antibiotics, and primary dysfunction of Meibomian glands alters the composition of this mixture, resulting in altered tear film stability and function. Korb and Henriquez coined the term meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD) in a study addressing contact lens intolerance and the obstruction of the Meibomian gland orifices by desquamated epithelial cells.[8] The International Workshop on MGD defined the disease as “a chronic, diffuse abnormality of the meibomian glands, commonly characterized by terminal duct obstruction and/or qualitative/ quantitative changes in the glandular secretion. It may result in alteration of the tear film, symptoms of eye irritation, clinically apparent inflammation, and ocular surface disease.”[9] Images of normal and progressive gland loss in patients with MGD are shown in Figure 2.[10] Figure 2. Images demonstrating representative cases of each grade of the meibomian gland changes. The upper and lower eyelids were turned over and meibomian glands were observed using an infrared transmitting filter and an infrared charge-coupled device video camera. Changes in meibomian glands were scored using the following grades in each eyelid (meiboscore): grade 0, no loss of meibomian glands; grade 1, area loss was less than one third of the total meibomian gland area; grade 2, area loss was between one third and two thirds; grade 3, area loss was more than two thirds. Reprinted with permission from American Academy of Ophthalmology from the article by Arita, Reiko et al (2008), Noncontact Infrared Meibography to Document Age-Related Changes of the Meibomian Glands in a Normal Population Ophthalmology, 115: 911-915. Epidemiology Meibomian gland dysfunction is an underdiagnosed and undertreated disease with asymptomatic disease being far more common than the symptomatic MGD.[11][12] It is estimated that 70% of Americans over the age of 60 have MGD.[13] The prevalence is lower among certain populations, ranging widely depending on the parameter looked at.[14][15] For example, prevalence may be 61.0–69.3% if based on telaniectasia in Asian populations, but it ranges from 3.5–19.9% among Caucasian populations. The prevalence increases with age and appears to be higher in males than in females. Risk Factors Risk factors for MGD include aging, deficiency of sex hormones (notably androgens), and systemic conditions such as Sjogren syndrome, Stevens-Johnson Syndrome, psoriasis, atopy, polycystic ovary syndrome, and hypertension.[4][10][16] In addition, certain ophthalmic factors have been shown to impact Meibomian gland function, namely aniridia, chronic blepharitis, contact lens wear, eyelid tattooing, trachoma, and Demodex folliculorum infestation . Use of antibiotics, isotretinoin for acne, antihistamines, antidepressants, and hormone replacement therapy are found to be associated with MGD. Classification Figure 3. Classification of MGD. Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2011;52:1930-7. The MGD classification system proposed by the 2011 International Workshop on MGD is shown in Figure 3.[9] Meibomian gland dysfunction is classified based on the final consequence of dry eye diseases (DED) as low delivery or high delivery, which refers to the secretion status. Meibomian gland obstruction, the most common cause for hyposecretion, results from the hypertrophy of ductal epithelium and keratinization due to aging, decreased expression of androgen receptors, or medication use. fetched_contents.text: Meibomian Gland Disease - StatPearls Continuing Education Activity Meibomian gland dysfunction encompasses various disorders affecting the meibomian glands, causing ocular discomfort, dry eyes, and visual disturbances. Factors like aging, digital device use, and hormonal changes contribute to its onset. Blocked meibomian ducts lead to reduced lipid secretion, tear film instability, and ocular surface inflammation. Diagnosis relies on outpatient tests and questionnaires to determine disease severity, guiding treatment decisions. Clinicians participating in this activity can expect to gain comprehensive insights into the condition, including its diverse etiology, pathophysiology, evaluation, and management strategies. Clinicians enhance their ability to recognize and diagnose meibomian gland dysfunction promptly, allowing for early intervention and improved patient outcomes. Specifically, they learn to identify risk factors associated with meibomian gland dysfunction, understand the impact of blocked meibomian ducts on tear film stability, and interpret key clinical indicators of disease severity. Moreover, clinicians become proficient in utilizing outpatient tests and patient questionnaires to guide treatment decisions tailored to patients' needs. Ultimately, participation in this activity empowers healthcare professionals with the knowledge and skills to manage meibomian gland dysfunction effectively, thereby enhancing the quality of care provided to patients suffering from this common ocular condition. Objectives: * Identify the clinical manifestations of meibomian gland disease during patient examinations. * Screen patients for meibomian gland disease using appropriate diagnostic tools and assessments. * Implement evidence-based treatment plans for managing meibomian gland disease in clinical practice. * Collaborate with other healthcare professionals to optimize comprehensive care for patients with meibomian gland disease. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic. Introduction Meibomian gland disease encompasses a range of meibomian gland disorders, including meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD), neoplasia, and congenital disease. MGD refers to the abnormalities in the function of the meibomian glands. The International Workshop on MGD describes MGD as a "chronic diffuse abnormality of the meibomian glands, characterized by terminal duct obstruction along with qualitative or quantitative changes in the glandular secretion."[1] Dysfunction in meibomian gland secretion can adversely influence the amount and quality of secreted meibum, leading to alterations in tear film composition and compromising ocular surface health. This can result in tear film abnormalities, ocular surface inflammation or irritation, or ocular surface disease.[2] Named after the German physician and anatomist Heinrich Meibom, the meibomian glands are sebaceous glands in the eyelid.[3] The upper lid contains approximately 20 to 30 meibomian glands, and the lower lid has 40 to 50.[4] These glands lie parallel in a single row within the tarsal plates of the upper and lower lids, with the proximal ends of the meibomian glands extending toward the proximal margin of the tarsal plates. The distal end of the tarsus receives meibum through the excretory duct into the lid margin. Meibum, composed primarily of lipids, stabilizes the tear film by lowering the surface tension, acts as a lubricant during blinking, prevents excessive evaporation of the tear film's aqueous layer, and provides an outer barrier that prevents bacteria from entering the tear film.[5] MGD is considered acute or chronic based on the duration of symptoms. Secretion rates of the glands determine further categorization. Low delivery states, or meibomian sicca, are due to gland hyposecretion or cicatricial or noncicatricial obstruction.[6] High delivery states, or meibomian seborrhea, involve gland hypersecretion, as noted in patients with acne rosacea or seborrheic dermatitis.[7] These states are then further divided into primary and secondary causes. Etiology The most common type of MGD is the obstructive form, resulting from obstruction of the meibomian gland terminal duct. Obstruction occurs due to ductal epithelium hypertrophy, keratinization, and the viscous nature of meibum. The result is atrophy and dropout of the meibomian glands, thus decreasing secretion. Meibomian gland atrophy and medication effects cause meibomian sicca. Atrophy of meibomian glands results in an overall reduction in functional meibomian glands. ## Branch report: recommended evaluations and objective tests for MGD

### Which physical exam findings should be assessed for MGD
The evidence strongly supports examining lid-margin appearance as a central physical exam finding for MGD. StatPearls notes that “red lid margins” suggest meibomian gland dysfunction and describes lid examination as part of the diagnostic workup [N1-F1]. The same source also emphasizes lid margin abnormality score as part of a proposed diagnostic approach for MGD [N1-R4]. Other relevant signs include lid vascularity and changes in meibum appearance, which are described as part of the meibomian gland dysfunction clinical presentation [N1-F2]. The EyeWiki entry also describes changes in meibomian glands, including gland atrophy, obstruction, changes in meibum quality, and eyelid vascularity, as clinically relevant findings [N1-F2].

### Which tear function and ocular surface tests are recommended
Tear function testing is central to evaluating MGD. The evidence repeatedly mentions tear break-up time (TBUT) as a core test. StatPearls states that TBUT is normal 15 to 45 seconds, borderline 10 to 15 seconds, and abnormal less than 10 seconds, and that TBUT is used in the dry eye workup [N2-R1]. It also notes Schirmer test and fluorescein break-up time (FBUT) as part of the evaluation framework [N2-R1]. The dry eye workup page explicitly includes TBUT and MGD grading as key components of the workup, with TBUT being tied to tear film instability [N2-R2]. EyeWiki similarly states that TBUT is normal 15–45 seconds, FBUT normal >10 seconds, and that TBUT is used in assessing disease severity [N2-R5]. A related study excerpt notes that tear-film break-up time was 9.6 seconds in one group and 4.6 seconds in another, showing how TBUT is used to assess tear film instability [N2-R4].

Ocular surface staining is also recommended. The dry eye workup page explicitly includes ocular surface staining as part of the assessment package [N2-R2]. EyeWiki similarly describes fluorescein break-up time and staining as part of the clinical evaluation [N2-R5]. This suggests that staining is used to identify ocular surface damage and tear film instability rather than as a standalone MGD test.

### Which imaging or advanced diagnostic tools are preferred
Imaging tools are increasingly preferred for more objective assessment of MGD. Meibography is explicitly described as an imaging technique that allows observation of the silhouette of the meibomian gland morphological structure [N4-R2]. EyeWiki notes that noncontact infrared meibography is used to document age-related changes and that meiboscore grading is based on meibography [N1-F2]. The same source also describes meiboscore as a semiquantitative grading system based on noncontact meibography [N6-R2]. LipiScan is presented as an advanced diagnostic tool for MGD, providing high-definition imaging of the meibomian glands and enabling precise diagnosis [N4-R3]. Another source describes LipiScan as “precise diagnosis” of MGD and as an important tool for managing dry eye disease [N4-R5]. Meibography and LipiScan are therefore the preferred advanced diagnostic tools in the evidence set, with meibography used for morphological assessment and LipiScan for more detailed imaging.

## Bottom line for this branch
The recommended evaluations for MGD are a combination of physical lid-margin assessment, tear function testing with TBUT and FBUT, ocular surface staining, and imaging with meibography and LipiScan. The evidence does not uniformly rank one method as the single best tool; rather, it supports a staged approach in which lid examination and TBUT provide initial clues, while meibography and LipiScan offer more objective, quantitative assessment [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence is moderately strong for TBUT and lid-margin findings, and somewhat stronger for imaging tools when they are used to document morphological changes [N1-F2][N6-R2][N4-R2].

## Branch report: implementation and evidence quality

### Which recommendations are based on strong versus weak evidence
The evidence set suggests a mix of strong, moderate, and weak evidence. The most directly authoritative guidance comes from the EyeWiki page and the AAO-related material, which describe current clinical practice and proposed diagnostic criteria [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R4]. These are likely best interpreted as current clinical consensus rather than randomized controlled trials, but they provide a strong practical framework because they are derived from major ophthalmology resources. In contrast, the evidence on imaging and grading includes more specialized studies and tool descriptions, which are useful but not as strong as guideline-based recommendations [N4-R2][N4-R3][N6-R2].

The evidence also shows that some recommendations are weakly supported by the provided snippets. For example, the dry eye workup page lists TBUT, MGD grading, and staining as key components, but the excerpt does not provide a detailed evidence rating or reference level of evidence [N2-R2]. Similarly, the proposed grading systems in the search results are described as novel or integrated scales, which suggests they are promising but not yet proven in the evidence provided [N6-R3][N6-R4]. The management guidance from StatPearls and EyeWiki is also practical and consensus-based rather than high-level evidence [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### How practice guidelines translate into routine clinical workup
In practice, guidelines translate into a stepwise clinical workup. The evidence supports starting with a detailed history and physical examination, including lid-margin signs and meibomian gland appearance [N1-F1][N1-F2]. TBUT is then used to assess tear film instability [N2-R1][N2-R5]. If the clinical suspicion remains, meibography or LipiScan is preferred for more objective morphological assessment [N4-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence also indicates that grading systems such as meiboscore are used to stage or grade MGD, which helps guide treatment decisions [N1-F2][N6-R2]. This means the guideline-based workup is not a single test but a sequence of assessments, with imaging reserved for cases where morphology or severity is unclear.

The AAO-related material and the proposed diagnostic criteria emphasize that the ocular symptom score, lid margin abnormality score, and meiboscore are used together in diagnosing MGD [N1-R4]. This reflects a practical, multi-step approach in routine care rather than a single laboratory test [N1-F1]. The dry eye workup page similarly presents TBUT and MGD grading as part of a broader diagnostic process, which is consistent with everyday clinical workflow [N2-R2].

### Common pitfalls and limitations in diagnosing MGD
Several limitations and pitfalls emerge from the evidence. One major pitfall is relying on TBUT alone to diagnose MGD. While TBUT is a core test for tear film instability, the evidence shows that shorter TBUT is associated with more meibomian gland dropout [N2-R3], which implies that TBUT may not distinguish MGD from other causes of tear film instability. Another limitation is that lid-margin signs can be nonspecific. StatPearls notes that red lid margins suggest MGD, but this sign is also associated with other conditions such as blepharitis and lid margin disease [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence also shows that lid margin abnormalities can be caused by medications, contact lenses, eyelid tattooing, and systemic conditions, so it is important not to assume MGD without further objective assessment [N1-F2].

A second pitfall is overreliance on subjective grading. The meiboscore is described as a semiquantitative score based on noncontact meibography [N6-R2], which means it is useful for staging but may be operator-dependent. The evidence also suggests that grading systems are still evolving, with newer proposals aiming to integrate clinical manifestations with severity [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This indicates that grading can be inconsistent across clinicians and should not be used in isolation.

Imaging and advanced tools also have limitations. Meibography and LipiScan are more objective, but they are not always available, and the evidence provided does not establish their superiority over clinical examination in all settings [N4-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that MGD is an underdiagnosed and undertreated disease, implying that even with better tools, many cases may be missed in routine practice [N1-F2]. In addition, the evidence indicates that MGD may coexist with other conditions, such as blepharitis, acne rosacea, and Demodex infestation, which can complicate diagnosis [N1-F2][N2-F3].

## Bottom line for this branch
The recommendations are strongest for TBUT, lid-margin assessment, and meibography/LipiScan, but they are mostly consensus-based rather than high-level evidence [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. Routine clinical workup should therefore follow a stepwise approach: history and physical examination first, then TBUT and staining, followed by imaging if morphology or severity is unclear [N2-R2][N2-R5]. Common pitfalls include using TBUT alone, overinterpreting lid-margin signs, relying on subjective grading, and failing to recognize that MGD may coexist with other lid-margin or systemic conditions [N2-R3][N1-F1][N1-F2].

## Branch report: clinical criteria and classification of MGD

### Which diagnostic criteria are currently used to classify MGD
The evidence indicates that current classification and diagnostic criteria for MGD are built around a combination of clinical signs, grading systems, and staging. The most directly cited current criterion is the proposed diagnostic approach that uses the ocular symptom score, lid margin abnormality score, and meiboscore to diagnose MGD [N1-R4]. EyeWiki also states that the International Workshop on MGD defines MGD as “a chronic, diffuse abnormality of the meibomian glands, commonly characterized by terminal duct obstruction and/or qualitative/quantitative changes in the glandular secretion” [N1-F2]. This definition is central to the current clinical framework.

In addition, the AAO-related material describes MGD as being classified based on the final consequence of dry eye diseases as low delivery or high delivery, with low delivery further divided into hyposecretory and obstructive conditions [N1-F2]. It also notes that obstructive MGD is the most common cause of hyposecretion and can be further classified into cicatricial and noncicatricial types [N1-F2]. EyeWiki similarly states that the MGD classification system proposed by the 2011 International Workshop on MGD is shown in a figure, with MGD classified by the consequences of dry eye disease [N1-F2].

### How MGD staging or grading is applied in practice
Staging or grading is applied mainly through meiboscore and related grading systems. EyeWiki describes meiboscore as a semiquantitative score of noncontact meibography results, with grades 0 through 3 indicating increasing loss of meibomian glands [N1-F2][N6-R2]. The same source notes that changes in meibomian glands are scored using these grades, with grade 0 indicating no loss and grade 3 indicating more than two thirds loss [N1-F2]. This means that grading is used to quantify the severity of gland loss rather than just confirming the presence of MGD.

The evidence also points to newer grading systems as attempts to improve staging. One search result describes a proposed new grading system to define MGD severity and classify patients by disease severity [N6-R3]. Another describes a comprehensive grading scale to evaluate clinical manifestations in patients with varying severity [N6-R4]. These systems suggest that grading is increasingly being used to support individualized treatment decisions, even though the evidence provided does not establish a single universally accepted grading standard.

### Whether the criteria distinguish MGD from other meibomian pathologies
The criteria do not fully distinguish MGD from other meibomian pathologies in the provided evidence, but they do attempt to differentiate the main categories. The International Workshop definition emphasizes terminal duct obstruction and/or qualitative/quantitative changes in secretion as central features of MGD [N1-F2]. This helps distinguish MGD from other meibomian disorders by focusing on gland function rather than only morphology. EyeWiki also notes that MGD includes obstructive forms, hyposecretory forms, and hypersecretory forms, with obstructive MGD being the most common cause of hyposecretion [N1-F2]. It further states that cicatricial MGD is caused by trachoma, erythema multiforme, and pemphigoid, while noncicatricial MGD is often associated with acne rosacea, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, and psoriasis [N1-F2].

This classification helps distinguish MGD from other meibomian conditions by identifying whether the pathology is obstructive, cicatricial, hyposecretory, or hypersecretory [N1-F2]. However, the evidence also shows that many of these conditions overlap with lid-margin disease, blepharitis, and Demodex infestation [N1-F2][N2-F3]. Therefore, the criteria do not fully exclude other meibomian pathologies, but they do provide a structured way to classify MGD and related disorders.

## Bottom line for this branch
Current diagnostic criteria for MGD combine clinical signs, grading systems, and staging. The most explicit criteria are the ocular symptom score, lid margin abnormality score, and meiboscore [N1-R4]. Classification is based on the International Workshop definition and subsequent categorization into low delivery/high delivery, hyposecretory/obstructive, and cicatricial/noncicatricial forms [N1-F2]. Meiboscore is used to stage or grade severity by quantifying gland loss [N1-F2][N6-R2]. The criteria are useful for distinguishing MGD from other meibomian pathologies, but they do not fully exclude overlap with blepharitis, lid-margin disease, and other conditions [N1-F2][N2-F3].

## Branch report: dry eye disease context and association

### How MGD is linked to dry eye disease in current guidelines
The evidence is clear that MGD is the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease and is deeply embedded in current guidelines. The AAO-related material states that MGD is the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease (DED) and is characterized by reduction and/or change in meibum secretion [N1-R5]. EyeWiki similarly describes MGD as a chronic, diffuse abnormality of the meibomian glands that may result in alteration of the tear film, symptoms of eye irritation, clinically apparent inflammation, and ocular surface disease [N1-F2]. The same source also states that MGD is classified based on the final consequence of dry eye diseases as low delivery or high delivery, which refers to secretion status [N1-F2].

A separate review explicitly frames MGD as a major contributor to dry eye disease, with the goal of providing a simplified approach to diagnose evaporative dry eye due to MGD and individualize treatment [N3-R4]. This shows that current guidelines and review literature treat MGD not as a separate entity but as a core mechanism of evaporative dry eye.

### Which dry eye subtypes or phenotypes are most commonly associated with MGD
The evidence suggests that evaporative dry eye is most directly associated with MGD, but it also points to broader dry eye phenotypes. The AAO-related material identifies MGD as the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease [N1-R5]. The dry eye workup page notes that ocular surface disease is a multifactorial condition characterized by tear film instability, inflammation, and damage to the ocular surface [N3-R3]. The same source also lists symptoms such as dryness, burning, itching, tearing, and foreign body sensation as part of the dry eye picture [N3-R3]. The review on dry eye phenotypes further states that the clinical picture in late disease differs in both severity and phenotype, implying that MGD is one of several phenotypes that evolve with disease progression [N8-R4].

The evidence also suggests that MGD is often associated with systemic or lid-margin conditions. EyeWiki notes that noncicatricial MGD is often associated with acne rosacea, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, and psoriasis [N1-F2]. It also lists risk factors such as Sjögren syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, psoriasis, atopy, and Demodex folliculorum infestation [N1-F2]. This indicates that MGD may occur in patients with dry eye phenotypes linked to inflammation, immune disease, or lid-margin pathology rather than only in a single, uniform dry eye subtype.

### What role ocular surface disease severity plays in diagnosis
Ocular surface disease severity is an important diagnostic and therapeutic consideration. The evidence states that dry eye disease is defined as a multifactorial disease of the tears and ocular surface resulting in symptoms of discomfort, visual disturbance, and tear film instability [N8-R1]. It also notes that tear film osmolarity was found to be the single best marker of disease severity across normal, mild/moderate, and severe categories [N8-R2]. This means severity is not only a clinical endpoint but also a guide to treatment intensity.

The evidence further supports that severity affects how dry eye is managed. The dry eye workup page describes a stepwise approach that uses TBUT, MGD grading, and staining, implying that severity is assessed alongside morphology [N2-R2]. The AAO-related material and proposed diagnostic criteria also suggest that staging or grading helps guide treatment decisions [N1-R4][N1-F2]. In addition, the review on dry eye phenotypes notes that the clinical picture in late disease differs in severity and phenotype, reinforcing that severity is a meaningful dimension of disease progression [N8-R4].

## Bottom line for this branch
Current guidelines and review literature treat MGD as the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease and as a central mechanism of ocular surface disease [N1-R5][N1-F2][N3-R4]. The most commonly associated dry eye phenotype is evaporative dry eye, but the evidence also points to broader phenotypes involving inflammation, immune disease, and lid-margin conditions [N3-R3][N8-R4]. Ocular surface disease severity plays a major role in diagnosis because tear film instability, inflammation, and osmolarity are used to assess severity, and severity guides treatment intensity [N8-R1][N8-R2]. Overall, MGD is best understood as a specific pathophysiological driver of dry eye, not a standalone dry eye type [N1-R5][N1-F2].

## 1) Current clinical criteria for classifying MGD

### What criteria are currently used?
The evidence indicates that current MGD diagnosis and classification combine clinical signs, grading systems, and staging. The most directly cited current diagnostic approach is the proposed use of the **ocular symptom score**, **lid margin abnormality score**, and **meiboscore** to diagnose MGD [N1-R4]. EyeWiki also states that the International Workshop on MGD defines MGD as “a chronic, diffuse abnormality of the meibomian glands, commonly characterized by terminal duct obstruction and/or qualitative/quantitative changes in the glandular secretion” [N1-F2]. This definition is central to current clinical criteria.

### How MGD staging or grading is applied in practice
Staging or grading is mainly applied through **meiboscore** and related grading systems. EyeWiki describes meiboscore as a **semiquantitative score** of noncontact meibography results, with grades 0 through 3 indicating increasing loss of meibomian glands: grade 0 means no loss, grade 1 means less than one third loss, grade 2 means between one third and two thirds loss, and grade 3 means more than two thirds loss [N1-F2][N6-R2]. This means grading is used to quantify severity rather than just confirm disease.

The evidence also points to newer grading systems as attempts to improve staging. One search result describes a proposed new grading system to define MGD severity and classify patients by disease severity [N6-R3], while another describes a comprehensive grading scale to evaluate clinical manifestations in patients with varying severity [N6-R4]. These systems suggest that grading is becoming more integrated into clinical decision-making, even though the evidence provided does not establish a single universally accepted standard.

### Do the criteria distinguish MGD from other meibomian pathologies?
The criteria do not fully exclude overlap with other meibomian pathologies, but they do attempt to distinguish the main categories. The International Workshop definition emphasizes terminal duct obstruction and/or qualitative/quantitative changes in secretion as central features of MGD [N1-F2]. EyeWiki also notes that MGD includes **obstructive**, **hyposecretory**, and **hypersecretory** forms, with obstructive MGD being the most common cause of hyposecretion [N1-F2]. It further states that cicatricial MGD is caused by trachoma, erythema multiforme, and pemphigoid, while noncicatricial MGD is often associated with acne rosacea, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, and psoriasis [N1-F2].

This classification helps distinguish MGD from other meibomian conditions by identifying whether the pathology is obstructive, cicatricial, hyposecretory, or hypersecretory [N1-F2]. However, the evidence also shows that many of these conditions overlap with lid-margin disease, blepharitis, and Demodex infestation [N1-F2][N2-F3]. So the criteria are useful for classification, but they do not fully exclude other meibomian or lid-margin disorders.

---

## 2) Recommended evaluations and objective tests

### Which physical exam findings should be assessed
The evidence strongly supports examining **lid-margin appearance** as a central physical exam finding for MGD. StatPearls notes that **red lid margins** suggest MGD and describes lid examination as part of the diagnostic workup [N1-F1]. The same source also emphasizes lid margin abnormality score as part of a proposed diagnostic approach [N1-R4]. Other relevant findings include lid vascularity and changes in meibum appearance, which are described as part of the meibomian gland dysfunction clinical presentation [N1-F2].

### Which tear function and ocular surface tests are recommended
Tear function testing is central. The evidence repeatedly mentions **tear break-up time (TBUT)** as a core test. StatPearls states that TBUT is normal 15 to 45 seconds, borderline 10 to 15 seconds, and abnormal less than 10 seconds, and that TBUT is used in the dry eye workup [N2-R1]. The dry eye workup page explicitly includes TBUT and MGD grading as key components of the workup, with TBUT tied to tear film instability [N2-R2]. EyeWiki similarly states that TBUT is normal 15–45 seconds and that it is used in assessing disease severity [N2-R5]. A related study excerpt notes that tear-film break-up time was 9.6 seconds in one group and 4.6 seconds in another, showing how TBUT is used to assess tear film instability [N2-R4].

Ocular surface staining is also recommended. The dry eye workup page explicitly includes ocular surface staining as part of the assessment package [N2-R2]. EyeWiki similarly describes fluorescein break-up time and staining as part of the clinical evaluation [N2-R5]. This suggests staining is used to identify ocular surface damage and tear film instability rather than as a standalone MGD test.

### Which imaging or advanced diagnostic tools are preferred
Imaging tools are increasingly preferred for more objective assessment of MGD. **Meibography** is explicitly described as an imaging technique that allows observation of the silhouette of the meibomian gland morphological structure [N4-R2]. EyeWiki notes that noncontact infrared meibography is used to document age-related changes and that meiboscore grading is based on meibography [N1-F2]. The same source also describes meiboscore as a semiquantitative grading system based on noncontact meibography [N6-R2]. **LipiScan** is presented as an advanced diagnostic tool for MGD, providing high-definition imaging of the meibomian glands and enabling precise diagnosis [N4-R3]. Another source describes LipiScan as “precise diagnosis” of MGD and as an important tool for managing dry eye disease [N4-R5].

So the preferred advanced diagnostic tools are **meibography** and **LipiScan**, with meibography used for morphological assessment and LipiScan for more detailed imaging [N4-R2][N4-R3].

---

## 3) How MGD is linked to dry eye disease in current guidelines

The evidence is clear that MGD is the **leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease** and is deeply embedded in current guidelines. The AAO-related material states that MGD is the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease (DED) and is characterized by reduction and/or change in meibum secretion [N1-R5]. EyeWiki similarly describes MGD as a chronic, diffuse abnormality of the meibomian glands that may result in alteration of the tear film, symptoms of eye irritation, clinically apparent inflammation, and ocular surface disease [N1-F2]. The same source also states that MGD is classified based on the final consequence of dry eye diseases as low delivery or high delivery, which refers to secretion status [N1-F2].

A separate review explicitly frames MGD as a major contributor to dry eye disease, with the goal of providing a simplified approach to diagnose evaporative dry eye due to MGD and individualize treatment [N3-R4]. This shows that current guidelines and review literature treat MGD not as a separate entity but as a core mechanism of evaporative dry eye.

---

## 4) Which dry eye subtypes or phenotypes are most commonly associated with MGD

The evidence suggests that **evaporative dry eye** is most directly associated with MGD, but it also points to broader dry eye phenotypes. The AAO-related material identifies MGD as the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease [N1-R5]. The dry eye workup page notes that ocular surface disease is a multifactorial condition characterized by tear film instability, inflammation, and damage to the ocular surface [N3-R3]. The same source also lists symptoms such as dryness, burning, itching, tearing, and foreign body sensation as part of the dry eye picture [N3-R3].

The evidence also suggests that MGD is often associated with systemic or lid-margin conditions. EyeWiki notes that noncicatricial MGD is often associated with acne rosacea, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, and psoriasis [N1-F2]. It also lists risk factors such as Sjögren syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, psoriasis, atopy, and Demodex folliculorum infestation [N1-F2]. This indicates that MGD may occur in patients with dry eye phenotypes linked to inflammation, immune disease, or lid-margin pathology rather than only in a single, uniform dry eye subtype.

---

## 5) What role ocular surface disease severity plays in diagnosis

Ocular surface disease severity is an important diagnostic and therapeutic consideration. The evidence states that dry eye disease is defined as a multifactorial disease of the tears and ocular surface resulting in symptoms of discomfort, visual disturbance, and tear film instability [N8-R1]. It also notes that tear film osmolarity was found to be the single best marker of disease severity across normal, mild/moderate, and severe categories [N8-R2]. This means severity is not only a clinical endpoint but also a guide to treatment intensity.

The evidence further supports that severity affects how dry eye is managed. The dry eye workup page describes a stepwise approach that uses TBUT, MGD grading, and staining, implying that severity is assessed alongside morphology [N2-R2]. The AAO-related material and proposed diagnostic criteria also suggest that staging or grading helps guide treatment decisions [N1-R4][N1-F2]. In addition, the review on dry eye phenotypes notes that the clinical picture in late disease differs in severity and phenotype, reinforcing that severity is a meaningful dimension of disease progression [N8-R4].

---

## 6) Implementation and evidence quality

### Which recommendations are based on strong versus weak evidence?
The evidence set suggests a mix of strong, moderate, and weak evidence. The most directly authoritative guidance comes from the EyeWiki page and the AAO-related material, which describe current clinical practice and proposed diagnostic criteria [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R4]. These are likely best interpreted as current clinical consensus rather than randomized controlled trials, but they provide a strong practical framework because they are derived from major ophthalmology resources. In contrast, the evidence on imaging and grading includes more specialized studies and tool descriptions, which are useful but not as strong as guideline-based recommendations [N4-R2][N4-R3][N6-R2].

The evidence also shows that some recommendations are weakly supported by the provided snippets. For example, the dry eye workup page lists TBUT, MGD grading, and staining as key components, but the excerpt does not provide a detailed evidence rating or reference level of evidence [N2-R2]. Similarly, the proposed grading systems in the search results are described as novel or integrated scales, which suggests they are promising but not yet proven in the evidence provided [N6-R3][N6-R4]. The management guidance from StatPearls and EyeWiki is also practical and consensus-based rather than high-level evidence [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### How practice guidelines translate into routine clinical workup
In practice, guidelines translate into a **stepwise clinical workup**. The evidence supports starting with a detailed history and physical examination, including lid-margin signs and meibomian gland appearance [N1-F1][N1-F2]. TBUT is then used to assess tear film instability [N2-R1][N2-R5]. If the clinical suspicion remains, **meibography** or **LipiScan** is preferred for more objective morphological assessment [N4-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence also indicates that grading systems such as meiboscore are used to stage or grade MGD, which helps guide treatment decisions [N1-F2][N6-R2]. This means the guideline-based workup is not a single test but a sequence of assessments, with imaging reserved for cases where morphology or severity is unclear.

### Common pitfalls and limitations in diagnosing MGD
Several limitations and pitfalls emerge from the evidence. One major pitfall is relying on **TBUT alone** to diagnose MGD. While TBUT is a core test for tear film instability, the evidence shows that shorter TBUT is associated with more meibomian gland dropout [N2-R3], which implies that TBUT may not distinguish MGD from other causes of tear film instability. Another limitation is that **lid-margin signs can be nonspecific**. StatPearls notes that red lid margins suggest MGD, but this sign is also associated with other conditions such as blepharitis and lid margin disease [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence also shows that lid margin abnormalities can be caused by medications, contact lenses, eyelid tattooing, and systemic conditions, so it is important not to assume MGD without further objective assessment [N1-F2].

A second pitfall is overreliance on **subjective grading**. The meiboscore is described as a semiquantitative score based on noncontact meibography [N6-R2], which means it is useful for staging but may be operator-dependent. The evidence also suggests that grading systems are still evolving, with newer proposals aiming to integrate clinical manifestations with severity [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This indicates that grading can be inconsistent across clinicians and should not be used in isolation.

Imaging and advanced tools also have limitations. **Meibography** and **LipiScan** are more objective, but they are not always available, and the evidence provided does not establish their superiority over clinical examination in all settings [N4-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that MGD is an underdiagnosed and undertreated disease, implying that even with better tools, many cases may be missed in routine practice [N1-F2]. In addition, the evidence indicates that MGD may coexist with other conditions, such as blepharitis, acne rosacea, and Demodex infestation, which can complicate diagnosis [N1-F2][N2-F3].

---

## 7) Bottom line for MGD associated with dry eye disease

### Clinical criteria
Current clinical criteria for MGD combine **clinical signs**, **grading systems**, and **staging**. The most explicit criteria are the **ocular symptom score**, **lid margin abnormality score**, and **meiboscore** [N1-R4]. Classification is based on the International Workshop definition and subsequent categorization into low delivery/high delivery, hyposecretory/obstructive, and cicatricial/noncicatricial forms [N1-F2]. Meiboscore is used to stage or grade severity by quantifying gland loss [N1-F2][N6-R2].

### Recommended evaluations
Recommended evaluations include a detailed **history and physical examination**, especially **lid-margin appearance** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The core tear function test is **TBUT**, with **normal 15–45 seconds**, **borderline 10–15 seconds**, and **abnormal less than 10 seconds** [N2-R1][N2-R5]. Ocular surface staining is also recommended to identify ocular surface damage and tear film instability [N2-R2][N2-R5]. Imaging tools such as **meibography** and **LipiScan** are preferred for more objective morphological assessment [N4-R2][N4-R3].

### Dry eye disease context
MGD is the **leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease** and is deeply embedded in current guidelines [N1-R5][N1-F2]. It is most commonly associated with **evaporative dry eye**, but the evidence also points to broader phenotypes involving **inflammation, immune disease, and lid-margin conditions** [N3-R3][N8-R4]. Ocular surface disease severity plays a major role in diagnosis and treatment because **tear film instability, inflammation, and osmolarity** are used to assess severity, and severity guides treatment intensity [N8-R1][N8-R2].

### Evidence quality and implementation
The evidence is strongest for **TBUT**, **lid-margin assessment**, and **meibography/LipiScan**, but much of the guidance is consensus-based rather than high-level evidence [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. Routine clinical workup should follow a **stepwise approach**: history and physical examination first, then TBUT and staining, followed by imaging if morphology or severity is unclear [N2-R2][N2-R5]. Common pitfalls include using TBUT alone, overinterpreting lid-margin signs, relying on subjective grading, and failing to recognize that MGD may coexist with other lid-margin or systemic conditions [N2-R3][N1-F1][N1-F2].

### Final synthesis
For MGD associated with dry eye disease, the current approach is best summarized as:
- **Diagnose with clinical signs plus objective tests**,
- **Stage or grade with meiboscore and related grading systems**,
- **Use TBUT and staining as core tear function tests**,
- **Use meibography and LipiScan for more objective imaging**,
- **Treat as a central driver of evaporative dry eye**, not a separate dry eye type [N1-R5][N1-F2][N3-R4].

The evidence supports a practical, staged workup rather than a single definitive test, and it cautions that MGD diagnosis can be complicated by overlap with other lid-margin or systemic conditions [N1-F2][N2-F3].

### Which recommendations are based on strong versus weak evidence
The evidence set suggests a mix of strong, moderate, and weak evidence. The most directly authoritative guidance comes from the EyeWiki page and the AAO-related material, which describe current clinical practice and proposed diagnostic criteria [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R4]. These are likely best interpreted as current clinical consensus rather than randomized controlled trials, but they provide a strong practical framework because they are derived from major ophthalmology resources. In contrast, the evidence on imaging and grading includes more specialized studies and tool descriptions, which are useful but not as strong as guideline-based recommendations [N4-R2][N4-R3][N6-R2].

The evidence also shows that some recommendations are weakly supported by the provided snippets. For example, the dry eye workup page lists TBUT, MGD grading, and staining as key components, but the excerpt does not provide a detailed evidence rating or reference level of evidence [N2-R2]. Similarly, the proposed grading systems in the search results are described as novel or integrated scales, which suggests they are promising but not yet proven in the evidence provided [N6-R3][N6-R4]. The management guidance from StatPearls and EyeWiki is also practical and consensus-based rather than high-level evidence [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### How practice guidelines translate into routine clinical workup
In practice, guidelines translate into a stepwise clinical workup. The evidence supports starting with a detailed history and physical examination, including lid-margin signs and meibomian gland appearance [N1-F1][N1-F2]. TBUT is then used to assess tear film instability [N2-R1][N2-R5]. If the clinical suspicion remains, meibography or LipiScan is preferred for more objective morphological assessment [N4-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence also indicates that grading systems such as meiboscore are used to stage or grade MGD, which helps guide treatment decisions [N1-F2][N6-R2]. This means the guideline-based workup is not a single test but a sequence of assessments, with imaging reserved for cases where morphology or severity is unclear.

The AAO-related material and the proposed diagnostic criteria emphasize that the ocular symptom score, lid margin abnormality score, and meiboscore are used together in diagnosing MGD [N1-R4]. This reflects a practical, multi-step approach in routine care rather than a single laboratory test [N1-F1]. The dry eye workup page similarly presents TBUT and MGD grading as part of a broader diagnostic process, which is consistent with everyday clinical workflow [N2-R2].

### Common pitfalls and limitations in diagnosing MGD
Several limitations and pitfalls emerge from the evidence. One major pitfall is relying on TBUT alone to diagnose MGD. While TBUT is a core test for tear film instability, the evidence shows that shorter TBUT is associated with more meibomian gland dropout [N2-R3], which implies that TBUT may not distinguish MGD from other causes of tear film instability. Another limitation is that lid-margin signs can be nonspecific. StatPearls notes that red lid margins suggest MGD, but this sign is also associated with other conditions such as blepharitis and lid margin disease [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence also shows that lid margin abnormalities can be caused by medications, contact lenses, eyelid tattooing, and systemic conditions, so it is important not to assume MGD without further objective assessment [N1-F2].

A second pitfall is overreliance on subjective grading. The meiboscore is described as a semiquantitative score based on noncontact meibography [N6-R2], which means it is useful for staging but may be operator-dependent. The evidence also suggests that grading systems are still evolving, with newer proposals aiming to integrate clinical manifestations with severity [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This indicates that grading can be inconsistent across clinicians and should not be used in isolation.

Imaging and advanced tools also have limitations. Meibography and LipiScan are more objective, but they are not always available, and the evidence provided does not establish their superiority over clinical examination in all settings [N4-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that MGD is an underdiagnosed and undertreated disease, implying that even with better tools, many cases may be missed in routine practice [N1-F2]. In addition, the evidence indicates that MGD may coexist with other conditions, such as blepharitis, acne rosacea, and Demodex infestation, which can complicate diagnosis [N1-F2][N2-F3].

## Bottom line for this branch
The recommendations are strongest for TBUT, lid-margin assessment, and meibography/LipiScan, but they are mostly consensus-based rather than high-level evidence [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. Routine clinical workup should therefore follow a stepwise approach: history and physical examination first, then TBUT and staining, followed by imaging if morphology or severity is unclear [N2-R2][N2-R5]. ### Which diagnostic criteria are currently used to classify MGD
The evidence indicates that current classification and diagnostic criteria for MGD are built around a combination of clinical signs, grading systems, and staging. The most directly cited current criterion is the proposed diagnostic approach that uses the ocular symptom score, lid margin abnormality score, and meiboscore to diagnose MGD [N1-R4]. EyeWiki also states that the International Workshop on MGD defines MGD as “a chronic, diffuse abnormality of the meibomian glands, commonly characterized by terminal duct obstruction and/or qualitative/quantitative changes in the glandular secretion” [N1-F2]. This definition is central to the current clinical framework.

In addition, the AAO-related material describes MGD as being classified based on the final consequence of dry eye diseases as low delivery or high delivery, with low delivery further divided into hyposecretory and obstructive conditions [N1-F2]. It also notes that obstructive MGD is the most common cause of hyposecretion and can be further classified into cicatricial and noncicatricial types [N1-F2]. EyeWiki similarly states that the MGD classification system proposed by the 2011 International Workshop on MGD is shown in a figure, with MGD classified by the consequences of dry eye disease [N1-F2].

### How MGD staging or grading is applied in practice
Staging or grading is applied mainly through meiboscore and related grading systems. EyeWiki describes meiboscore as a semiquantitative score of noncontact meibography results, with grades 0 through 3 indicating increasing loss of meibomian glands [N1-F2][N6-R2]. The same source notes that changes in meibomian glands are scored using these grades, with grade 0 indicating no loss and grade 3 indicating more than two thirds loss [N1-F2]. This means that grading is used to quantify the severity of gland loss rather than just confirming the presence of MGD.

The evidence also points to newer grading systems as attempts to improve staging. One search result describes a proposed new grading system to define MGD severity and classify patients by disease severity [N6-R3]. Another describes a comprehensive grading scale to evaluate clinical manifestations in patients with varying severity [N6-R4]. These systems suggest that grading is increasingly being used to support individualized treatment decisions, even though the evidence provided does not establish a single universally accepted grading standard.

### Whether the criteria distinguish MGD from other meibomian pathologies
The criteria do not fully distinguish MGD from other meibomian pathologies in the provided evidence, but they do attempt to differentiate the main categories. The International Workshop definition emphasizes terminal duct obstruction and/or qualitative/quantitative changes in secretion as central features of MGD [N1-F2]. This helps distinguish MGD from other meibomian disorders by focusing on gland function rather than only morphology. EyeWiki also notes that MGD includes obstructive forms, hyposecretory forms, and hypersecretory forms, with obstructive MGD being the most common cause of hyposecretion [N1-F2]. It further states that cicatricial MGD is caused by trachoma, erythema multiforme, and pemphigoid, while noncicatricial MGD is often associated with acne rosacea, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, and psoriasis [N1-F2].

This classification helps distinguish MGD from other meibomian conditions by identifying whether the pathology is obstructive, cicatricial, hyposecretory, or hypersecretory [N1-F2]. However, the evidence also shows that many of these conditions overlap with lid-margin disease, blepharitis, and Demodex infestation [N1-F2][N2-F3]. Therefore, the criteria do not fully exclude other meibomian pathologies, but they do provide a structured way to classify MGD and related disorders.

## Bottom line for this branch
Current diagnostic criteria for MGD combine clinical signs, grading systems, and staging. The most explicit criteria are the ocular symptom score, lid margin abnormality score, and meiboscore [N1-R4]. Classification is based on the International Workshop definition and subsequent categorization into low delivery/high delivery, hyposecretory/obstructive, and cicatricial/noncicatricial forms [N1-F2]. Meiboscore is used to stage or grade severity by quantifying gland loss [N1-F2][N6-R2]. The criteria are useful for distinguishing MGD from other meibomian pathologies, but they do not fully exclude overlap with blepharitis, lid-margin disease, and other conditions [N1-F2][N2-F3].

### How MGD is linked to dry eye disease in current guidelines
The evidence is clear that MGD is the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease and is deeply embedded in current guidelines. The same source also states that MGD is classified based on the final consequence of dry eye diseases as low delivery or high delivery, which refers to secretion status [N1-F2].

A separate review explicitly frames MGD as a major contributor to dry eye disease, with the goal of providing a simplified approach to diagnose evaporative dry eye due to MGD and individualize treatment [N3-R4]. This shows that current guidelines and review literature treat MGD not as a separate entity but as a core mechanism of evaporative dry eye.

### Which dry eye subtypes or phenotypes are most commonly associated with MGD
The evidence suggests that evaporative dry eye is most directly associated with MGD, but it also points to broader dry eye phenotypes. The AAO-related material identifies MGD as the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease [N1-R5]. The dry eye workup page notes that ocular surface disease is a multifactorial condition characterized by tear film instability, inflammation, and damage to the ocular surface [N3-R3]. The same source also lists symptoms such as dryness, burning, itching, tearing, and foreign body sensation as part of the dry eye picture [N3-R3]. The review on dry eye phenotypes further states that the clinical picture in late disease differs in both severity and phenotype, implying that MGD is one of several phenotypes that evolve with disease progression [N8-R4].

The evidence also suggests that MGD is often associated with systemic or lid-margin conditions. EyeWiki notes that noncicatricial MGD is often associated with acne rosacea, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, and psoriasis [N1-F2]. It also lists risk factors such as Sjögren syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, psoriasis, atopy, and Demodex folliculorum infestation [N1-F2]. This indicates that MGD may occur in patients with dry eye phenotypes linked to inflammation, immune disease, or lid-margin pathology rather than only in a single, uniform dry eye subtype.

### What role ocular surface disease severity plays in diagnosis
Ocular surface disease severity is an important diagnostic and therapeutic consideration. The evidence states that dry eye disease is defined as a multifactorial disease of the tears and ocular surface resulting in symptoms of discomfort, visual disturbance, and tear film instability [N8-R1]. It also notes that tear film osmolarity was found to be the single best marker of disease severity across normal, mild/moderate, and severe categories [N8-R2]. This means severity is not only a clinical endpoint but also a guide to treatment intensity.

The evidence further supports that severity affects how dry eye is managed. The dry eye workup page describes a stepwise approach that uses TBUT, MGD grading, and staining, implying that severity is assessed alongside morphology [N2-R2]. The AAO-related material and proposed diagnostic criteria also suggest that staging or grading helps guide treatment decisions [N1-R4][N1-F2]. ## Bottom line for this branch
Current guidelines and review literature treat MGD as the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease and as a central mechanism of ocular surface disease [N1-R5][N1-F2][N3-R4]. The most commonly associated dry eye phenotype is evaporative dry eye, but the evidence also points to broader phenotypes involving inflammation, immune disease, and lid-margin conditions [N3-R3][N8-R4]. Ocular surface disease severity plays a major role in diagnosis because tear film instability, inflammation, and osmolarity are used to assess severity, and severity guides treatment intensity [N8-R1][N8-R2]. Overall, MGD is best understood as a specific pathophysiological driver of dry eye, not a standalone dry eye type [N1-R5][N1-F2].

## Branch report: recommended evaluations and objective tests for MGD

### Which physical exam findings should be assessed for MGD
The evidence strongly supports examining lid-margin appearance as a central physical exam finding for MGD. StatPearls notes that “red lid margins” suggest meibomian gland dysfunction and describes lid examination as part of the diagnostic workup [N1-F1]. The same source also emphasizes lid margin abnormality score as part of a proposed diagnostic approach for MGD [N1-R4]. Other relevant signs include lid vascularity and changes in meibum appearance, which are described as part of the meibomian gland dysfunction clinical presentation [N1-F2]. The EyeWiki entry also describes changes in meibomian glands, including gland atrophy, obstruction, changes in meibum quality, and eyelid vascularity, as clinically relevant findings [N1-F2].

### Which tear function and ocular surface tests are recommended
Tear function testing is central to evaluating MGD. The evidence repeatedly mentions tear break-up time (TBUT) as a core test. StatPearls states that TBUT is normal 15 to 45 seconds, borderline 10 to 15 seconds, and abnormal less than 10 seconds, and that TBUT is used in the dry eye workup [N2-R1]. It also notes Schirmer test and fluorescein break-up time (FBUT) as part of the evaluation framework [N2-R1]. The dry eye workup page explicitly includes TBUT and MGD grading as key components of the workup, with TBUT being tied to tear film instability [N2-R2]. EyeWiki similarly states that TBUT is normal 15–45 seconds, FBUT normal >10 seconds, and that TBUT is used in assessing disease severity [N2-R5]. A related study excerpt notes that tear-film break-up time was 9.6 seconds in one group and 4.6 seconds in another, showing how TBUT is used to assess tear film instability [N2-R4].

Ocular surface staining is also recommended. The dry eye workup page explicitly includes ocular surface staining as part of the assessment package [N2-R2]. EyeWiki similarly describes fluorescein break-up time and staining as part of the clinical evaluation [N2-R5]. This suggests that staining is used to identify ocular surface damage and tear film instability rather than as a standalone MGD test.

### Which imaging or advanced diagnostic tools are preferred
Imaging tools are increasingly preferred for more objective assessment of MGD. Meibography is explicitly described as an imaging technique that allows observation of the silhouette of the meibomian gland morphological structure [N4-R2]. EyeWiki notes that noncontact infrared meibography is used to document age-related changes and that meiboscore grading is based on meibography [N1-F2]. The same source also describes meiboscore as a semiquantitative grading system based on noncontact meibography [N6-R2]. LipiScan is presented as an advanced diagnostic tool for MGD, providing high-definition imaging of the meibomian glands and enabling precise diagnosis [N4-R3]. Another source describes LipiScan as “precise diagnosis” of MGD and as an important tool for managing dry eye disease [N4-R5]. Meibography and LipiScan are therefore the preferred advanced diagnostic tools in the evidence set, with meibography used for morphological assessment and LipiScan for more detailed imaging.

## Bottom line for this branch
The recommended evaluations for MGD are a combination of physical lid-margin assessment, tear function testing with TBUT and FBUT, ocular surface staining, and imaging with meibography and LipiScan. The evidence does not uniformly rank one method as the single best tool; rather, it supports a staged approach in which lid examination and TBUT provide initial clues, while meibography and LipiScan offer more objective, quantitative assessment [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R5][N4-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence is moderately strong for TBUT and lid-margin findings, and somewhat stronger for imaging tools when they are used to document morphological changes [N1-F2][N6-R2][N4-R2].

## Branch report: implementation and evidence quality

### Which recommendations are based on strong versus weak evidence
The evidence set suggests a mix of strong, moderate, and weak evidence. The most directly authoritative guidance comes from the EyeWiki page and the AAO-related material, which describe current clinical practice and proposed diagnostic criteria [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R4]. These are likely best interpreted as current clinical consensus rather than randomized controlled trials, but they provide a strong practical framework because they are derived from major ophthalmology resources. In contrast, the evidence on imaging and grading includes more specialized studies and tool descriptions, which are useful but not as strong as guideline-based recommendations [N4-R2][N4-R3][N6-R2].

The evidence also shows that some recommendations are weakly supported by the provided snippets. For example, the dry eye workup page lists TBUT, MGD grading, and staining as key components, but the excerpt does not provide a detailed evidence rating or reference level of evidence [N2-R2]. Similarly, the proposed grading systems in the search results are described as novel or integrated scales, which suggests they are promising but not yet proven in the evidence provided [N6-R3][N6-R4]. The management guidance from StatPearls and EyeWiki is also practical and consensus-based rather than high-level evidence [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### How practice guidelines translate into routine clinical workup
In practice, guidelines translate into a stepwise clinical workup. The evidence supports starting with a detailed history and physical examination, including lid-margin signs and meibomian gland appearance [N1-F1][N1-F2]. TBUT is then used to assess tear film instability [N2-R1][N2-R5]. If the clinical suspicion remains, meibography or LipiScan is preferred for more objective morphological assessment [N4-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence also indicates that grading systems such as meiboscore are used to stage or grade MGD, which helps guide treatment decisions [N1-F2][N6-R2]. This means the guideline-based workup is not a single test but a sequence of assessments, with imaging reserved for cases where morphology or severity is unclear.

The AAO-related material and the proposed diagnostic criteria emphasize that the ocular symptom score, lid margin abnormality score, and meiboscore are used together in diagnosing MGD [N1-R4]. This reflects a practical, multi-step approach in routine care rather than a single laboratory test [N1-F1]. The dry eye workup page similarly presents TBUT and MGD grading as part of a broader diagnostic process, which is consistent with everyday clinical workflow [N2-R2].

### Common pitfalls and limitations in diagnosing MGD
Several limitations and pitfalls emerge from the evidence. One major pitfall is relying on TBUT alone to diagnose MGD. While TBUT is a core test for tear film instability, the evidence shows that shorter TBUT is associated with more meibomian gland dropout [N2-R3], which implies that TBUT may not distinguish MGD from other causes of tear film instability. Another limitation is that lid-margin signs can be nonspecific. StatPearls notes that red lid margins suggest MGD, but this sign is also associated with other conditions such as blepharitis and lid margin disease [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The evidence also shows that lid margin abnormalities can be caused by medications, contact lenses, eyelid tattooing, and systemic conditions, so it is important not to assume MGD without further objective assessment [N1-F2].

A second pitfall is overreliance on subjective grading. The meiboscore is described as a semiquantitative score based on noncontact meibography [N6-R2], which means it is useful for staging but may be operator-dependent. The evidence also suggests that grading systems are still evolving, with newer proposals aiming to integrate clinical manifestations with severity [N6-R3][N6-R4]. This indicates that grading can be inconsistent across clinicians and should not be used in isolation.

Imaging and advanced tools also have limitations. Meibography and LipiScan are more objective, but they are not always available, and the evidence provided does not establish their superiority over clinical examination in all settings [N4-R2][N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that MGD is an underdiagnosed and undertreated disease, implying that even with better tools, many cases may be missed in routine practice [N1-F2]. In addition, the evidence indicates that MGD may coexist with other conditions, such as blepharitis, acne rosacea, and Demodex infestation, which can complicate diagnosis [N1-F2][N2-F3].

## Bottom line for this branch
The recommendations are strongest for TBUT, lid-margin assessment, and meibography/LipiScan, but they are mostly consensus-based rather than high-level evidence [N1-F1][N1-F2][N2-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3]. Routine clinical workup should therefore follow a stepwise approach: history and physical examination first, then TBUT and staining, followed by imaging if morphology or severity is unclear [N2-R2][N2-R5]. Common pitfalls include using TBUT alone, overinterpreting lid-margin signs, relying on subjective grading, and failing to recognize that MGD may coexist with other lid-margin or systemic conditions [N2-R3][N1-F1][N1-F2].

## Branch report: clinical criteria and classification of MGD

### Which diagnostic criteria are currently used to classify MGD
The evidence indicates that current classification and diagnostic criteria for MGD are built around a combination of clinical signs, grading systems, and staging. The most directly cited current criterion is the proposed diagnostic approach that uses the ocular symptom score, lid margin abnormality score, and meiboscore to diagnose MGD [N1-R4]. EyeWiki also states that the International Workshop on MGD defines MGD as “a chronic, diffuse abnormality of the meibomian glands, commonly characterized by terminal duct obstruction and/or qualitative/quantitative changes in the glandular secretion” [N1-F2]. This definition is central to the current clinical framework.

In addition, the AAO-related material describes MGD as being classified based on the final consequence of dry eye diseases as low delivery or high delivery, with low delivery further divided into hyposecretory and obstructive conditions [N1-F2]. It also notes that obstructive MGD is the most common cause of hyposecretion and can be further classified into cicatricial and noncicatricial types [N1-F2]. EyeWiki similarly states that the MGD classification system proposed by the 2011 International Workshop on MGD is shown in a figure, with MGD classified by the consequences of dry eye disease [N1-F2].

### How MGD staging or grading is applied in practice
Staging or grading is applied mainly through meiboscore and related grading systems. EyeWiki describes meiboscore as a semiquantitative score of noncontact meibography results, with grades 0 through 3 indicating increasing loss of meibomian glands [N1-F2][N6-R2]. The same source notes that changes in meibomian glands are scored using these grades, with grade 0 indicating no loss and grade 3 indicating more than two thirds loss [N1-F2]. This means that grading is used to quantify the severity of gland loss rather than just confirming the presence of MGD.

The evidence also points to newer grading systems as attempts to improve staging. One search result describes a proposed new grading system to define MGD severity and classify patients by disease severity [N6-R3]. Another describes a comprehensive grading scale to evaluate clinical manifestations in patients with varying severity [N6-R4]. These systems suggest that grading is increasingly being used to support individualized treatment decisions, even though the evidence provided does not establish a single universally accepted grading standard.

### Whether the criteria distinguish MGD from other meibomian pathologies
The criteria do not fully distinguish MGD from other meibomian pathologies in the provided evidence, but they do attempt to differentiate the main categories. The International Workshop definition emphasizes terminal duct obstruction and/or qualitative/quantitative changes in secretion as central features of MGD [N1-F2]. This helps distinguish MGD from other meibomian disorders by focusing on gland function rather than only morphology. EyeWiki also notes that MGD includes obstructive forms, hyposecretory forms, and hypersecretory forms, with obstructive MGD being the most common cause of hyposecretion [N1-F2]. It further states that cicatricial MGD is caused by trachoma, erythema multiforme, and pemphigoid, while noncicatricial MGD is often associated with acne rosacea, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, and psoriasis [N1-F2].

This classification helps distinguish MGD from other meibomian conditions by identifying whether the pathology is obstructive, cicatricial, hyposecretory, or hypersecretory [N1-F2]. However, the evidence also shows that many of these conditions overlap with lid-margin disease, blepharitis, and Demodex infestation [N1-F2][N2-F3]. Therefore, the criteria do not fully exclude other meibomian pathologies, but they do provide a structured way to classify MGD and related disorders.

## Bottom line for this branch
Current diagnostic criteria for MGD combine clinical signs, grading systems, and staging. The most explicit criteria are the ocular symptom score, lid margin abnormality score, and meiboscore [N1-R4]. Classification is based on the International Workshop definition and subsequent categorization into low delivery/high delivery, hyposecretory/obstructive, and cicatricial/noncicatricial forms [N1-F2]. Meiboscore is used to stage or grade severity by quantifying gland loss [N1-F2][N6-R2]. The criteria are useful for distinguishing MGD from other meibomian pathologies, but they do not fully exclude overlap with blepharitis, lid-margin disease, and other conditions [N1-F2][N2-F3].

## Branch report: dry eye disease context and association

### How MGD is linked to dry eye disease in current guidelines
The evidence is clear that MGD is the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease and is deeply embedded in current guidelines. The AAO-related material states that MGD is the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease (DED) and is characterized by reduction and/or change in meibum secretion [N1-R5]. EyeWiki similarly describes MGD as a chronic, diffuse abnormality of the meibomian glands that may result in alteration of the tear film, symptoms of eye irritation, clinically apparent inflammation, and ocular surface disease [N1-F2]. The same source also states that MGD is classified based on the final consequence of dry eye diseases as low delivery or high delivery, which refers to secretion status [N1-F2].

A separate review explicitly frames MGD as a major contributor to dry eye disease, with the goal of providing a simplified approach to diagnose evaporative dry eye due to MGD and individualize treatment [N3-R4]. This shows that current guidelines and review literature treat MGD not as a separate entity but as a core mechanism of evaporative dry eye.

### Which dry eye subtypes or phenotypes are most commonly associated with MGD
The evidence suggests that evaporative dry eye is most directly associated with MGD, but it also points to broader dry eye phenotypes. The AAO-related material identifies MGD as the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease [N1-R5]. The dry eye workup page notes that ocular surface disease is a multifactorial condition characterized by tear film instability, inflammation, and damage to the ocular surface [N3-R3]. The same source also lists symptoms such as dryness, burning, itching, tearing, and foreign body sensation as part of the dry eye picture [N3-R3]. The review on dry eye phenotypes further states that the clinical picture in late disease differs in both severity and phenotype, implying that MGD is one of several phenotypes that evolve with disease progression [N8-R4].

The evidence also suggests that MGD is often associated with systemic or lid-margin conditions. EyeWiki notes that noncicatricial MGD is often associated with acne rosacea, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, and psoriasis [N1-F2]. It also lists risk factors such as Sjögren syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, psoriasis, atopy, and Demodex folliculorum infestation [N1-F2]. This indicates that MGD may occur in patients with dry eye phenotypes linked to inflammation, immune disease, or lid-margin pathology rather than only in a single, uniform dry eye subtype.

### What role ocular surface disease severity plays in diagnosis

This shows that current guidelines and review literature treat MGD not as a separate entity but as a core mechanism of evaporative dry eye.

## 4) Which dry eye subtypes or phenotypes are most commonly associated with MGD

The evidence suggests that **evaporative dry eye** is most directly associated with MGD, but it also points to broader dry eye phenotypes. The AAO-related material identifies MGD as the leading cause of evaporative dry eye disease [N1-R5]. The dry eye workup page notes that ocular surface disease is a multifactorial condition characterized by tear film instability, inflammation, and damage to the ocular surface [N3-R3]. The same source also lists symptoms such as dryness, burning, itching, tearing, and foreign body sensation as part of the dry eye picture [N3-R3].

The evidence also suggests that MGD is often associated with systemic or lid-margin conditions. EyeWiki notes that noncicatricial MGD is often associated with acne rosacea, atopic dermatitis, seborrheic dermatitis, and psoriasis [N1-F2]. It also lists risk factors such as Sjögren syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, psoriasis, atopy, and Demodex folliculorum infestation [N1-F2]. This indicates that MGD may occur in patients with dry eye phenotypes linked to inflammation, immune disease, or lid-margin pathology rather than only in a single, uniform dry eye subtype.

## 5) What role ocular surface disease severity plays in diagnosis

Ocular surface disease severity is an important diagnostic and therapeutic consideration. The evidence states that dry eye disease is defined as a multifactorial disease of the tears and ocular surface resulting in symptoms of discomfort, visual disturbance, and tear film instability [N8-R1]. It also notes that tear film osmolarity was found to be the single best marker of disease severity across normal, mild/moderate, and severe categories [N8-R2]. This means severity is not only a clinical endpoint but also a guide to treatment intensity.

The evidence further supports that severity affects how dry eye is managed. The dry eye workup page describes a stepwise approach that uses TBUT, MGD grading, and staining, implying that severity is assessed alongside morphology [N2-R2]. The AAO-related material and proposed diagnostic criteria also suggest that staging or grading helps guide treatment decisions [N1-R4][N1-F2]. In addition, the review on dry eye phenotypes notes that the clinical picture in late disease differs in severity and phenotype, reinforcing that severity is a meaningful dimension of disease progression [N8-R4].
